content.value: Trace object references passed into and returned from methods. Distinguish changing a shared object from reassigning a local parameter.

Java passes every argument by value. For a primitive argument, the parameter gets a copy of the primitive value. For an object argument, the parameter gets a copy of the reference. Caller and parameter can therefore refer to the same mutable object. Calling a mutator through either reference changes that shared object. Reassigning the parameter changes only its local reference.

A method can return a reference to an existing object or a newly constructed object. Returning a reference to mutable private state gives the caller an alias. To protect independent state, a method can return a new object initialized with copied values. Returning a String does not let a caller change that String object in place, because Strings are immutable.

original and copy initially refer to the same Counter with count 4. increment changes that shared object to 5. The parameter is then reassigned to a different Counter; original still refers to the first object. The output is 5.

Pass-by-value does not prevent mutation of an object reached through a copied reference. In contrast, assigning a new object or null to the parameter does not reassign the caller variable. A method returning its stored Counter reference exposes the same Counter rather than automatically copying it.

Trace the example without copy.increment(). The output is 4. Now imagine Counter identity(Counter item) { return item; }. Calling it returns a reference to the very same object supplied by the caller.
